## Discussion

These results demonstrate that a memory model can explain many of the findings in the rodent electrophysiology literature that were previously assumed to reflect the operations of an entorhinal/hippocampal navigation system. By explaining navigation with a memory model, this provides unified account of the rodent navigation and human memory literatures. Furthermore, the model explains cell surveys of the rodent entorhinal that appear to indicate that most of the information flowing into rodent hippocampus is spatial. In the proposed account, the function of cells that exhibit a hexagonal spatial grid has been misclassified as spatial (see also Luo et al., 2024). In the model, place cells are memory cells, representing conjunctions of what and where, and grid cells are non-spatial what cells that fire at specific locations where the non-spatial attribute is remembered. In a typical rodent navigation study, there are diffuse non-spatial properties that may become associated with locations throughout the recording enclosure (e.g. electronic noise, lighting, fear, attached wires, etc.). Because there are many such properties, there are many grid cells. Some of the cells in entorhinal cortex are truly spatial on this account, such as head direction cells (including head direction conjunctive grid cells) and border cells. However, according to this memory model, grid cells without head direction sensitivity are non-spatial. These grid cells only appear to be spatial because their activity was recorded while the animal navigated an enclosure in which the non-spatial attributes were the same at all locations. The uniformity of the non-spatial attributes leads to a situation in which memories become arrayed in a hexagonal grid owing to pattern separation.

In a typical rodent spatial navigation study, the non-spatial attributes are well-controlled, existing at all locations regardless of the enclosure used during testing (hence, a grid cell in one enclosure will be a grid cell in a different enclosure). Because labs adopt standard procedures, the surfaces, odors (e.g. from cleaning), external lighting, time of day, human handler, electronic apparatus, hunger/thirst state, etc. might be the same for all recording sessions. Additionally, the animal is not allowed to interact with other animals during recording and this isolation may be an unusual and highly salient property of all recording sessions. Notably, the animal is always attached to wires during recording. The internal state of the animal (fear, aloneness, the noise of electronics, etc.) is likely similar across all recording situations and attributes of this internal state are likely represented in the hippocampus and entorhinal input to hippocampus. According to this model, hippocampal place cells are ‘marking’ all locations in the enclosure as places where these things tend to happen.

In terms of the animal’s internal state, all locations in the enclosure may be viewed as equally aversive and unrewarding, which is a memorable characteristic of the enclosure. Reward, or lack thereof, is arguably one of the most important non-spatial characteristics and application of this model to reward might explain the existence of goal-related activity in place cells (Hok et al., 2007; although see Duvelle et al., 2019), reflecting the need to remember rewarding locations for goal directed behavior. Furthermore, if place cell memories for a rewarding location activate entorhinal grid cells, this may explain the finding that grid cells remap in an enclosure with a rewarded location such that firing fields are attracted to that location (Boccara et al., 2019; Butler et al., 2019). Studies that introduce reward into the enclosure are an important first step in terms of examining what happens to grid cells when the animal is placed in a more varied environment.

### Key predictions made by this memory model

Future studies should investigate what happens to grid cells when rodents navigate in truly naturalistic settings that include varied objects, varied food sources, varied surfaces, other animals, etc. Do grid cells persist in such a naturalistic environment (perhaps some of them will persist, considering that the animal is still subjected to the electronic recording apparatus and other lab procedures)? Or will some grid cells lose their regularity, or even become silent, considering that there is no longer uniformity to the non-spatial attributes? The results of Barry et al., 2012 demonstrate that the grid pattern expands and becomes less regular in a novel environment. Nevertheless, the novel environment in that study was uncluttered rather than naturalistic.

A key prediction of this account is that in the absence of memory retrieval from hippocampal place cells, each mEC grid cell should revert to its underlying bottom-up receptive field. For instance, in the absence of top-down memory retrieval feedback, a head direction conjunctive grid cell should become a head direction cell at all positions rather than just at grid field positions. Such a finding was reported by Bonnevie et al., 2013. More generally, this kind of result should occur for all grid cells. For instance, if the bottom-up receptive field for a grid cell is a tuning function for a preferred sound frequency, then that cell should exhibit sound frequency sensitivity in all positions in absence of hippocampal feedback rather than only responding in remembered positions. In brief, this account assumes that all grid cells are conjunctive grid cells except that the nature of the non-spatial attribute that makes them conjunctive is not yet known for many grid cells (see Aronov et al., 2017, for an example of what might be sound conjunctive grid cells).

This model predicts that place cell fields should be arrayed in a hexagonal grid for situations that produce grid cell firing. This does not mean that all place cell fields should be part of the same grid. Instead, the key prediction is that sets of place cells should be arrayed in a grid where a set of place cells is defined as place cells that represent the same attribute in conjunction with location information (e.g. all places with a particular sound). The attribute that links a set of place cells could be spatial, such as with head direction (i.e. a remembered viewpoint at all locations), and one way to test this idea would be to find sets of place cells that are sensitive to the same head direction, with a test of whether their corresponding place fields are arrayed in a grid. A different approach to testing this prediction could determine co-activity between grid cells and place cells (e.g., find the set of place cells that are co-active with a particular grid cell). Once a set of place cells is identified in this manner, the place field centers of the set should be arrayed in the same manner as the grid cell used to identify the set. In other words, there should be a one-to-one correspondence between each grid field of a particular grid cell and a corresponding place field.

The one-to-one correspondence grid fields and place fields arises from hippocampal feedback in the model. In other words, the place fields are the cause of the grid fields. However, the model is bidirectional and recurrent. For instance, memory consolidation of the place cells arises from cycles of bottom-up and top-down activation between entorhinal cells and hippocampal place cells. As such, changes in the properties of the grid cells may entail changes in the properties of place cells. This recurrence might explain the finding that manipulations of grid spacing are associated with an increase in the size of place fields (Mallory et al., 2018). For this memory model, place cell field size directly relates to the stability of place cells. If the place cells are actively moving their place centers with ongoing consolidation (e.g. moving to acquire a larger spacing between memories), they will appear to have larger place fields as they shift position. In the simulation results, this occurred with a novel enclosure (see for instance the larger grid field sizes, which arise from unstable place cells, for the novel network results in Figure 6, Figure 7), and to a lesser extent with remapping Appendix 1—figure 3.

According to this model, hexagonally arranged grid cells should be the exception rather than the rule when considering more naturalistic environments. In a more ecologically valid situation, such as with landmarks, varied sounds, food sources, threats, and interactions with conspecifics, there may still be remembered locations were events occurred or remembered properties can be found, but because the non-spatial properties are non-uniform in the environment, the arrangement of memory feedback will be irregular, reflecting the varied nature of the environment. This may explain the finding that even in a situation where there are regular hexagonal grid cells, there are often irregular non-grid cells that have a reliable multi-location firing field, but the arrangement of the firing fields is irregular (Diehl et al., 2017). For instance, even when navigating in an enclosure that has uniform properties as dictated by experimental procedures, they may be other properties that were not well-controlled (e.g. a view of exterior lighting in some locations but not others), and these uncontrolled properties may produce an irregular grid (i.e. because the uncontrolled properties are reliably associated with some locations but not others, hippocampal memory feedback triggers retrieval of those properties in the associations locations).

In this memory model, there are other situations in which an irregular but reliable multi-location grid may occur, even when everything is well controlled. In the reported simulations, when the hippocampal place cells were based on variation in X/Y (as defined by Border cells), nothing else changed as a function of location, and the model rapidly produced a precise hexagonal arrangement of hippocampal place cell memories. When head direction was included (i.e. real-world variation in X, Y, and head direction), the model still produced a hexagonal arrangement as per face-centered cubic packing of memories, but this precise arrangement was slower to emerge, with place cells continuing to shift their positions until the borders of the enclosure were sufficiently well learned from multiple viewpoints. If there is real-world variation in four or more dimensions, as is likely the case in a more ecologically valid situation, it will be even harder for place cell memories to settle on a precise regular lattice. Furthermore, in the case of four dimensions, mathematicians studying the ‘sphere packing problem’ recently concluded that densest packing is irregular (Campos et al., 2023). This may explain why the multifield grid cells for freely flying bats have a systematic minimum distance between firing fields, but their arrangement is globally irregular (Ginosar et al., 2021). Assuming that the memories encoded by a bat include not just the three real-world dimensions of variation, but also head direction, the grid will likely be irregular even under optimal conditions of laboratory control.

This memory model predicts that grid-like responses do not require spatial navigation for their existence. Instead, grid-like responses might occur in any situation involving a highly familiar two-dimensional space in which nothing of interest varies aside from the two dimensions. In such cases, the memories that represent points in the two-dimensional space arrange themselves into an equally spaced hexagonal pattern owing to consolidation and pattern separation. If this pattern separation consolidation process is a general property of cortical neurons, grid-like responses may be found throughout the cortex. This might explain why well-learned non-spatial two-dimensional spaces such as cartoon bird neck/leg length (Constantinescu et al., 2016) and pine/banana odors (Bao et al., 2019) produce grid-like responses in areas other than the MTL. It might also explain why visual search in the two dimensions of the visual field can produce grid-like responses in humans (Julian et al., 2018) and primates (Killian et al., 2012).

### Other grid cell models assume that spatial grid cells have a spatial function

The regularity of grid cell responses is fascinating and unparalleled in neuroscience – the existence of the grid pattern assuredly tells us something important about the operation of the nervous system and, correspondingly, there have been dozens of models aimed at explaining how the regular grid pattern emerges. These models are briefly considered to highlight the most important differences between them and this memory model of grid cells.

The first wave of grid cell models built the grid cell responses in a purely bottom-up fashion, proposing that place cells learn their positions as defined by a population code of grid cells (Hasselmo, 2009; Mhatre et al., 2012; Solstad et al., 2006). Subsequent work called into question these models (although see Lian and Burkitt, 2022), based on the finding that inactivation of the hippocampus eliminates grid responses (Bonnevie et al., 2013) and the finding that place cells exist before grid cells during development (Bjerknes et al., 2014). To accommodate such results, a second wave of grid cell models assumed that place cells serve as a guide for the development/emergence of grid cell responses (Castro and Aguiar, 2014; Stepanyuk, 2015; Widloski and Fiete, 2014). However, it is less clear why the grid cells are needed in these models, considering that place cells could directly provide spatial knowledge, although some have proposed that grid cells are useful for charting novel navigational paths (Bellmund et al., 2016; Bush et al., 2015; Sorscher et al., 2023). Another class of grid cell models propose that the grid emerges from intrinsic attractor dynamics within entorhinal cortex (Burak and Fiete, 2009; Couey et al., 2013; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; Guanella et al., 2007; McNaughton et al., 2006), explaining why the grid can exist even during sleep (Gardner et al., 2019). However, in these models, the function of entorhinal grid cells is nevertheless assumed to support spatial representations.

Recently, there are several models that take a broader information-theoretic view of the MTL by asking what kinds of representations are useful for representing different kinds of spaces in a parsimonious manner (Bellmund et al., 2018; Mok and Love, 2019; Rodríguez-Domínguez and Caplan, 2019; Wei et al., 2015), or useful for predictive coding (Stachenfeld et al., 2017). These models can capture some of the grid cell results presented in the current simulations, including extension to non-spatial grid-like responses (e.g. grid field that cover a two-dimensional neck/leg length bird space). Furthermore, these models may be able to explain memory phenomena similar to the model proposed in this study. However, unlike the proposed model, these models assume that the function of entorhinal grid cells that exhibit spatial X/Y grid fields during navigation is to represent space. In contrast, the memory model proposed in this study assume that the function of spatial X/Y grid cells is to represent a non-spatial attribute; the only reason they exhibit a spatial X/Y grid is because memories of that non-spatial attribute are arranged in a hexagonal grid owing to the uncluttered/unvarying nature of the enclosure. Thus, these model do not explain why most of the input to rodent hippocampus appears to be spatial (Boccara et al., 2010; Diehl et al., 2017; Grieves and Jeffery, 2017), whereas the proposed model can explain this situation as reflecting the miss-classification of grid cells with a spatial arrangement as providing spatial input to hippocampus.

### Conclusions

Returning to the original question posed in this study – how can the function of the MTL be the creation and retrieval of episodic memories if most of the cells in MTL are spatial? The proposed theory and model present a potential answer. The appearance of rodent MTL as primarily concerned with navigation rather than memory may be spurious if grid cells have been misclassified as spatial. Instead, place cells may be ‘memory cells’ that combine spatial location with many other dimensions into complex conjunctions representing episodic memories, and the precise hexagonal firing pattern of grid cells might reflect memory encoding for non-spatial attributes (‘what’) that are found throughout the two-dimensional surface.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.95733.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.95733.3.sa2)

The author presents a novel theory and computational model suggesting that grid cells do not encode space, but rather encode non-spatial attributes. Place cells in turn encode memories of where those specific attributes occurred. The theory accounts for many experimental results and generates useful predictions for future studies. The model's simplicity and potential explanatory power will interest others in the field. There are, however, a few weaknesses outlined below which undermine the theory.

Main criticisms:

(1) A crucial assumption of the model is that grid cells express grid-like firing patterns if and only if the content of experience is constant in space. It is difficult to imagine a real world example that satisfies this assumption. Odors and sounds are used as examples. While they are often more spatially diffuse than an object on the ground, odors and sounds have sources that are readily detectable and thus are not constant in space. Animals can easily navigate to a food source or to a vocalizing conspecific. This assumption is especially problematic because it predicts that all grid cells should become silent when their preferred non-spatial attribute (e.g. a specific odor) is missing. I'm not aware of any experimental data showing that grid cells become silent. On the contrary, grid cells are known to remain active across all contexts that have been tested, including across sleep/wake states. Unlike place cells, grid cells have never been shown to turn off. Since grid cells are active in all contexts, their preferred attribute must also be present in all contexts, and therefore they would not convey any information about the specific content of an experience. The author lists many attributes that could in theory be constant in a laboratory setting, but there is no data I'm aware of that shows this is true in practice. As it stands, this crucial assumption of the model remains mere speculation.

(2) The proposed novelty of this theory is that other models all assume that grid cells encode space. This is not quite true of models based on continuous attractor networks, the discussion of which is essentially absent. More specifically, attractor models focus on the importance of intrinsic dynamics within entorhinal cortex in generating the grid pattern. While this firing pattern is aligned to space during navigation and therefore can be used a representation of that space, the neural dynamics are preserved even during sleep. Similarly, it is because the grid pattern does not strictly encode physical space that grid-like signals are also observed in relation to other two-dimensional continuous variables.

(3) The use of border cells or boundary vector cells as the main (or only) source of spatial information in the hippocampus is not well supported by experimental data. Border cells in entorhinal cortex are not active in the center of an environment. Boundary-vector cells can fire farther away from the walls, but are not found in entorhinal cortex. They are located in the subiculum, a major output of the hippocampus. While the entorhinal-hippocampal circuit is a loop, the route from boundary-vector cells to place cells is much less clear than from grid cells. Moreover, both border cells and boundary-vector cells (which are conflated in this paper) comprise a small population of neurons compared to grid cells.

Minor comments:

(1) There is substantial theoretical and experimental work supporting the idea that grid cell modules instantiate continuous attractor networks, yet this class of models is largely ignored:

(2) The author claims in two places that this model is the first to explain that grid cell population activity lies on a torus. While it may be the first explicit computational account of why grid cell activity is mapped onto a torus, these claims should be moderated for clarity, for example by adding "but see McNaughton et al. It should be considered that the predominance of spatial representations reported in the literature is due to historical reasons. results.result: The proposed memory model reinterprets grid cells as representing non-spatial attributes rather than spatial information, with place cells representing conjunctions of spatial and non-spatial attributes. Grid cells exhibit hexagonal spatial firing patterns due to feedback from hippocampal place cells arranged in a hexagonal lattice through memory consolidation processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C25 and C71 collectively describe the core theoretical framework of the model, which is internally consistent and clearly articulated. The model provides a novel interpretation that is logically coherent, though empirical validation of the non-spatial nature of grid cells remains a prediction rather than demonstrated fact.

results.result: The model architecture uses border cells as primary spatial input to hippocampus, with place cells recruited during memory formation using Hebbian-like learning. Memory consolidation through pattern separation produces equally dissimilar memories arranged in a hexagonal lattice.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 and C91-C100 describe the model architecture and learning mechanisms with appropriate citations to prior work. The model assumptions are clearly stated and mathematically specified, providing a coherent computational framework that can be implemented and tested.

results.result: Model simulations demonstrate that grid patterns emerge immediately in novel environments with specific geometric properties: non-spatial attribute cells show immediate hexagonal grids, head direction cells form modules with three layers following face-centered cubic packing, and interior place cells arrange in precise hexagonal patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C110 and C120 report specific simulation results with quantitative measures (grid scores, spacing ratios, cell counts). The results are internally consistent and supported by figures showing firing maps and spatial autocorrelations. However, the simulations test the model's internal consistency rather than providing empirical validation.

results.result: Simulations show differential time courses for grid field stabilization: non-spatial attribute cells produce immediate grid patterns while head direction cells require prior experience. Grid stabilization correlates with formation of exterior place cell memories that conform to enclosure borders.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C114 describe simulation results showing temporal dynamics of grid formation with reference to specific figures. The results are quantified with grid scores across sessions and demonstrate a mechanistic explanation for the differential stabilization rates. The findings are internally consistent with the model's assumptions.

results.result: Model simulations produce two types of place cells: 29 exterior place cells (active <2.5% of time) that fire near borders with high head direction selectivity, and 19 interior place cells (active >2.5%) with lower head direction selectivity, particularly at place field centers.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C119 report specific quantitative results from simulations with clear operational definitions (2.5% activity threshold). The results are supported by firing maps in Figure 10B showing the predicted properties. The findings follow logically from the model's consolidation mechanism.

results.result: The model explains empirical findings about grid and border cell responses to enclosure manipulations, including rotation effects that depend on enclosure geometry and deformation effects that affect only some grid modules.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33, C40, and C52 cite empirical findings and explain how the model accounts for them through its assumptions about border cell alignment and multiple grid modules. The explanations are logically consistent with the model architecture, though they rely on specific assumptions about border cell organization.

results.result: The model predicts that both place cells and grid cells lie on a toroidal manifold defined by circular border cell dimensions, providing one of the first computational explanations for the empirically observed toroidal population structure of grid cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C35, C72-C73, and C103 describe a model prediction that matches empirical findings (Gardner et al., 2022). The toroidal structure emerges naturally from the circular dimension assumptions. The claim of being 'one of the first' is appropriately hedged with citations to prior models.

results.result: The model makes testable predictions: grid cells should revert to their underlying non-spatial receptive fields without hippocampal feedback, place cell fields should be hexagonally arranged for situations producing grid cell firing, and there should be one-to-one correspondence between grid fields and place fields.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C84 clearly state testable predictions that follow logically from the model's core assumptions. C82 notes that one prediction (head direction cells becoming active at all positions without hippocampal feedback) has empirical support from Bonnevie et al., 2013, providing some validation.

results.result: The model predicts that hexagonal grid cells should be rare in naturalistic environments with varied non-spatial attributes, and that grid-like responses can occur in any highly familiar two-dimensional space without requiring spatial navigation.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C88 state predictions that follow from the model's core assumption that hexagonal grids emerge only when non-spatial attributes are uniform across space. C86 cites empirical support for irregular multi-location firing fields (Diehl et al., 2017), consistent with the prediction.

results.result: The model uses three non-orthogonal circular dimensions to achieve approximately Euclidean distance representations, in contrast to two orthogonal dimensions which produce city-block metrics.
results.evaluation: Claims C36, C92-C93 describe a design choice supported by empirical evidence that animals learn Euclidean representations (C36 with citations). Figure 3D demonstrates the Euclidean approximation quantitatively. The mathematical reasoning is sound and the choice is well-justified.

results.result: The model accounts for empirical findings about grid and place cell dynamics: grids are less regular in novel environments, grid spacing shrinks with experience, grids appear immediately upon entry to novel environments, place cells slowly stabilize, and boundary encounters stabilize grid fields.
results.evaluation: Claims C39, C41, C53-C55 cite multiple empirical findings and explain how the model accounts for them through consolidation dynamics and boundary learning. Each claim is supported by appropriate citations and the explanations are consistent with the model's mechanisms.

results.result: The model relates grid cell modules to dense sphere packing in three dimensions (Kepler conjecture), predicting face-centered cubic or hexagonal close packing arrangements. Empirical data shows modules with spacing ratios of √2, which differs from the model's predicted √3 ratio.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C51 describe empirical findings about grid modules and relate them to sphere packing theory. However, C51 notes a discrepancy between the model's prediction (√3 spacing ratio) and empirical observations (√2 ratio). The author proposes an alternative interpretation but this remains speculative and unvalidated.

results.result: The model explains grid-like responses in non-spatial domains (bird morphology space, odor space, visual search) as arising from the same memory consolidation mechanisms applied to two-dimensional non-spatial spaces.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62 cite empirical findings of grid-like responses in non-spatial domains and explain them through the model's general memory framework. The explanation is logically consistent with the model's assumptions, though it remains a post-hoc explanation rather than a prediction that was validated.

results.result: The model is consistent with findings that hippocampal inactivation eliminates grid responses and that place cells exist before grid cells during development, supporting the model's assumption that place cells drive grid cell responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 cite empirical findings that support the model's core assumption of hippocampal-to-entorhinal feedback. These findings are used to motivate the model architecture and are consistent with the model's predictions, though they were not generated by the model.

results.result: The model assumes that cells habituate to constant stimulation and adjust firing thresholds through divisive normalization and inhibitory interneurons, allowing grid cells to modulate activity based on memory feedback rather than constant bottom-up drive.
results.evaluation: Claims C38, C77-C78 describe model assumptions about neural adaptation mechanisms, with C38 and C78 supported by appropriate citations to habituation and normalization literature. The assumptions are biologically plausible and necessary for the model to produce the observed firing patterns.

results.result: The manuscript reviews prior literature establishing that MTL function differs between species (episodic memory in humans/primates vs. spatial navigation in rodents) and that spatial location is a powerful episodic retrieval cue, motivating the need for a unified memory-based account.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C10 accurately cite and summarize prior literature with appropriate references. The claims establish the scientific context and motivation for the proposed model. The literature review is balanced and acknowledges both memory and spatial navigation perspectives.

results.result: The manuscript correctly attributes the discovery of major cell types in the rodent navigation system: place cells (O'Keefe, 1976), grid cells (Hafting et al., 2005), head direction cells (Taube et al., 1990), conjunctive grid cells (Sargolini et al., 2006), border cells (Lever et al., 2009; Solstad et al., 2008), and object-vector cells (Høydal et al., 2019).
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C16 provide accurate historical attributions with appropriate citations. These are factual claims about the discovery of cell types that are well-established in the literature and correctly cited.

results.result: The manuscript reviews the functional distinction between lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC) providing non-spatial 'what' information, particularly about objects, and medial entorhinal cortex (mEC) providing spatial 'where' information, though acknowledging some overlap.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C19 and C89-C90 accurately summarize the literature on LEC/mEC functional distinctions with appropriate citations. The claims acknowledge nuance (LEC provides some spatial information) and are used to motivate the model's reinterpretation of mEC function.

results.result: The manuscript reviews empirical findings on head direction sensitivity in place cells, showing strong sensitivity in mazes and more complex sensitivity in open fields, and that removal of head direction input affects both place and grid cell responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 accurately cite empirical findings about head direction's role in place and grid cell responses. The citations are appropriate and the findings are used to justify including head direction as an input dimension in the model.

results.result: The manuscript cites memory principles (encoding in novel situations, retrieval in familiar situations, pattern separation during consolidation) and perceptual phenomena (caricature effects) to support the model's consolidation mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27 and C56-C57 cite established findings from memory and perception literature with appropriate references. These principles are used to motivate the model's learning rules, though the application to spatial navigation is novel.

results.result: The manuscript cites evidence for non-spatial representations in MTL across species and for temporal representations in hippocampus, acknowledging limitations of the current model in addressing temporal aspects of episodic memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 accurately cite literature on non-spatial and temporal representations with appropriate references. C67 is used to acknowledge a limitation of the current model, demonstrating appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: The manuscript cites findings about place field size changes with grid spacing manipulations, irregular grid patterns in flying bats, and mathematical results on sphere packing in four dimensions to support model predictions about irregular grids in higher-dimensional spaces.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 cite relevant empirical and mathematical findings with appropriate references. The citations support the model's predictions about when regular hexagonal grids should and should not emerge, though the connections are somewhat speculative.

results.result: The manuscript cites various supporting findings and methods (human reorientation difficulty, Grid Score measure, border cell properties, context effects, theta oscillations) that relate to model assumptions and predictions.
results.evaluation: Claims C34, C37, C74-C76, and C80 cite diverse literature that supports various aspects of the model or relates to its predictions. The citations are appropriate and accurately represent the cited work, though some connections (e.g., C80 on theta oscillations) are speculative.

results.result: The manuscript cites evidence that grid cells exist during sleep to contrast with the proposed memory model, which assumes grid patterns arise from memory feedback during active navigation.
results.evaluation: Claim C58 accurately cites Gardner et al., 2019 regarding grid cells during sleep. This finding is acknowledged as a challenge for the proposed model, which emphasizes memory retrieval during active navigation, demonstrating appropriate consideration of contradictory evidence.

results.result: The model assumes the enclosure width is half the period of circular border cells to reduce confusion between opposite sides of the enclosure.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 clearly states a specific model assumption with clear rationale. This design choice is necessary for the model to avoid confusing opposite borders and is explicitly acknowledged as an assumption rather than an empirical constraint.

results.result: The core theoretical proposal that place cells represent conjunctions of spatial and non-spatial attributes, while grid cells primarily represent non-spatial attributes found throughout the environment, with grid cells exhibiting spatial firing patterns due to feedback from hippocampal place cells. Hexagonal grids emerge as a special case when animals explore large, featureless surfaces.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the theory is 'impressive' and 'tightly integrating data' but express fundamental concerns. Reviewer 3 critiques the crucial assumption that grid cells encode non-spatial attributes constant in space, noting 'it is difficult to imagine a real world example' and that this 'remains mere speculation.' Reviewer 2 notes the model 'still focuses on explaining the spatial firing aspect of grid cells even though they are not supposed to be spatial,' indicating conceptual tension. The impact would be strengthened 'if future experiments reveal that grid cells do indeed encode specific nonspatial features.'

results.result: The model uses border cells as the primary spatial input to hippocampus that determines place coding, based on the boundary vector cell model. The model explains border cell rotation behavior in circular versus square environments and predicts cells that fire between borders.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 raises a significant concern that 'the use of border cells or boundary vector cells as the main (or only) source of spatial information in the hippocampus is not well supported by experimental data,' noting that 'border cells in entorhinal cortex are not active in the center of an environment' and 'comprise a small population of neurons compared to grid cells.' This challenges a foundational architectural assumption of the model.

results.result: The model predicts that place cells and grid cell population codes lie on a torus defined by circular border cells, explaining the toroidal nature of grid cells observed empirically.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes that while the model may be 'the first explicit computational account of why grid cell activity is mapped onto a torus,' the claims should be 'moderated for clarity' by acknowledging prior models (McNaughton et al., 2006; Guanella et al., 2007). The reviewer suggests adding qualifications like 'but see McNaughton et al. (2006) and others,' indicating the novelty claim is overstated.

results.result: The model addresses findings that grid cells exist during sleep, that hippocampal inactivation eliminates grid responses, and that place cells exist before grid cells during development, positioning itself relative to attractor network models.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes that 'discussion of [continuous attractor network models] is essentially absent' and that 'this class of models is largely ignored,' despite substantial theoretical and experimental support. The reviewer points out that attractor models already explain why 'the grid can exist even during sleep' and that 'grid-like signals are also observed in relation to other two-dimensional continuous variables,' suggesting the proposed model's treatment of alternative frameworks is incomplete.

results.result: The model predicts that without hippocampal feedback, grid cells should revert to their underlying bottom-up receptive fields, with head direction conjunctive grid cells becoming head direction cells at all positions rather than just at grid field positions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 acknowledges that the prediction about head direction conjunctive grid cells reverting to head direction cells 'was reported by Bonnevie et al., 2013,' indicating empirical support for this model prediction. This is presented as consistent evidence rather than challenged.

results.result: The model predicts that hexagonally arranged grid cells should be the exception rather than the rule in naturalistic environments, that grid-like responses do not require spatial navigation, and that they might occur in any highly familiar two-dimensional space where nothing varies aside from the two dimensions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'it is good to know that it captures data that show non-grid like responses in more complex and realistic environments' but expresses concern that 'the model still focuses on explaining the spatial firing aspect of grid cells even though they are not supposed to be spatial.' The reviewer finds the points 'fair' but indicates 'theoretical disagreements' remain about whether grid-like coding is truly a special case.

results.result: The model assumes LEC provides non-spatial 'what' information for memory encoding (particularly related to objects), while mEC provides spatial 'where' information, though LEC also provides some forms of spatial information.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 states 'lateral entorhinal cortex is largely ignored in this memory model' and notes that 'it is therefore confusing to assume that these attributes are instead encoded by grid cells' when LEC 'is known to encode odors, objects, and time in a way that medial entorhinal cortex does not.' Reviewer 2 also notes 'the difference between mEC and lEC or PRC for encoding non-spatial vs spatial attributes is still not clear to me.'

results.result: The model implementation uses three non-orthogonal circular dimensions to achieve approximately Euclidean memory similarity, with bidirectional weights between place cells and entorhinal inputs. Memory consolidation produces unbiased representations through pattern separation, pushing memories to become maximally dissimilar and forming equilateral triangles in two dimensions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'Thank you for providing a video - this makes it extremely clear how learning occurs,' indicating acceptance of the model's learning mechanisms. No reviewer challenges the technical implementation details or consolidation process, suggesting implicit acceptance of these methodological choices.

results.result: Simulation results showing that the model produces hexagonal grids with grid scores of 0.4 after 1000 timesteps in novel environments, that grids align with border cell directions, that head direction cells require prior experience to stabilize while non-spatial attribute cells produce immediate grids, and that place cells divide into exterior (border-selective, head-direction-selective) and interior (hexagonally arranged) populations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the model 'accounts for many experimental results' and is 'an impressive computational account of MTL cells.' Reviewer 2 explicitly thanks the author for the video clarifying learning, suggesting acceptance of the simulation results. No reviewer challenges the specific simulation outcomes or their internal consistency, though they question the underlying theoretical assumptions.

results.result: The model assumes that cells avoid constant maximal firing through habituation, divisive normalization, and inhibitory interneurons, allowing grid cells to fire preferentially at memory locations despite their non-spatial attribute being present everywhere.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'habituation happens, but then spatial cell responses are supposed (or assumed) to be still strong after many visits to that environment,' indicating concern about the consistency of this assumption. Reviewer 3 raises a related concern that if grid cells' preferred attributes are 'present in all contexts, they would not convey any information about the specific content of an experience.'

results.result: The model accounts for empirical findings that grid patterns are less regular in novel environments, align with enclosure walls, shrink with experience, appear immediately upon entry to novel environments, and that place cells take time to stabilize while boundary encounters stabilize grid fields.
results.evaluation: These claims reference established empirical findings that the model aims to explain. Reviewers note the theory 'accounts for many experimental results' without specifically challenging these particular explanations, suggesting acceptance that the model addresses these phenomena.

results.result: The model explains grid cell modules with the same orientation, spacing, and distortion but different phases, relating this to the Kepler conjecture about sphere packing (FCP and HCP arrangements), with grid spacing ratios of approximately √2 between modules and differential responses to enclosure deformation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the model 'tightly integrating data on various spatial cell types' and 'accounts for many experimental results.' The specific explanations of module organization and spacing ratios are not challenged, suggesting acceptance of these model features.

results.result: The model explains grid-like responses in non-spatial two-dimensional spaces such as bird morphology dimensions, odor spaces, and visual search in humans and primates.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note the model 'generates strong predictions for future studies' and acknowledge it addresses grid-like responses in non-spatial domains. Reviewer 2 agrees that 'grid-like and spatial coding are a special case - both in navigation and memory,' indicating acceptance that the model addresses these phenomena.

results.result: The model predicts that place cell fields should be arrayed in a hexagonal grid for situations that produce grid cell firing, with one-to-one correspondence between each grid field of a particular grid cell and a corresponding place field.
results.evaluation: These predictions follow logically from the model architecture where place cells cause grid fields. Reviewers note the model 'generates strong predictions for future studies that will be of interest to researchers in this field' without challenging these specific predictions.
